title: Arbitration and Conciliation Act s. 3 — Statutory provision (ACA s. 3)

content.overview: Section 3 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 governs receipt of written communications in arbitral proceedings, subject to party agreement and the statutory exceptions for judicial-authority proceedings.
content.glance: Section 3 establishes when a written communication is deemed received, including delivery to the addressee's person, place of business, habitual residence or mailing address, and the alternative last-known-address mechanism after reasonable inquiry.
content.study:
Section 3 — Receipt of written communications

Statutory rule
Unless otherwise agreed by the parties, section 3 creates statutory rules for deemed receipt of written communications in arbitral proceedings.

1. Ordinary route: A written communication is deemed received when delivered personally to the addressee or at the addressee's place of business, habitual residence or mailing address.
2. Alternative route: If none of those places can be found after reasonable inquiry, the communication is deemed received when sent to the addressee's last known place of business, habitual residence or mailing address by registered letter or another means providing a record of the attempt to deliver.
3. Date of receipt: Under section 3(2), the communication is deemed received on the day on which it is delivered.
4. Judicial proceedings excluded: Section 3(3) does not apply to written communications concerning proceedings of a judicial authority.

The section therefore concerns statutory receipt, not merely actual knowledge. The first question is whether the communication falls within section 3; the second is whether the statutory route to deemed receipt has been satisfied; and the third is whether the parties agreed to a different arrangement.

Section 3 must be applied to the communication and the record of delivery. A party relying on deemed receipt should preserve the delivery record, the address used, evidence of reasonable inquiry where the alternative route is invoked, and any contractual or procedural agreement modifying the default rule.

sections.heading: 1. Statutory structure
sections.body: Section 3(1) begins with the default phrase “Unless otherwise agreed by the parties”. The statutory scheme therefore operates subject to a contrary agreement. The ordinary route is personal delivery or delivery at the addressee's place of business, habitual residence or mailing address.

sections.heading: 2. Alternative last-known-address route
sections.body: Where none of the places identified in section 3(1)(a) can be found after reasonable inquiry, section 3(1)(b) permits deemed receipt through sending the communication to the addressee's last known place of business, habitual residence or mailing address by registered letter or another means that provides a record of the attempt to deliver. The reasonable-inquiry condition should be proved rather than assumed.

sections.heading: 3. Date of deemed receipt
sections.body: Section 3(2) fixes the deemed date of receipt as the day on which the communication is delivered. This matters where another provision or procedural step depends upon the date of receipt.

sections.heading: 4. Judicial-authority proceedings excluded
sections.body: Section 3(3) expressly removes written communications in respect of proceedings of a judicial authority from the operation of section 3. The section should therefore not be mechanically applied to court communications.

sections.heading: 5. Evidence and professional application
sections.body: A party relying on section 3 should identify the applicable delivery route, the address relied upon, the delivery record and, where section 3(1)(b) is invoked, the reasonable inquiry undertaken. The statutory deemed-receipt rule should be kept distinct from proof of the underlying merits of the dispute.

examples.title: Personal or designated-address delivery
examples.body: A notice is delivered personally to the addressee during the arbitral process. Subject to any contrary agreement and the other requirements of the Act, section 3(1)(a) treats the communication as received on the day it is delivered.

examples.title: Last-known-address route
examples.body: The addressee's place of business, habitual residence and mailing address cannot be found after reasonable inquiry. The sender uses a registered letter to the last known mailing address and retains the record of the attempt. Section 3(1)(b) supplies the alternative deemed-receipt route.

examples.title: Judicial communication
examples.body: A written communication concerns proceedings of a judicial authority rather than the arbitral proceeding. Section 3(3) excludes that communication from the statutory deemed-receipt rule.

hypotheticals.question: A party sends an arbitral communication to the respondent's last known address without first making reasonable inquiry about the respondent's current place of business, habitual residence or mailing address. Can section 3(1)(b) automatically deem receipt?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. The alternative route is conditioned on none of the places specified in section 3(1)(a) being found after reasonable inquiry. The sender must establish that statutory precondition before relying on the last-known-address mechanism.

hypotheticals.question: The parties agreed in their arbitration clause on a different method for receipt of written communications. Which rule applies?
hypotheticals.analysis: Section 3(1) is expressly subject to the words “Unless otherwise agreed by the parties”. The agreed method must therefore be examined before applying the default statutory route.

hypotheticals.question: A party seeks to use section 3 for a communication concerning court proceedings. Is section 3 applicable?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. Section 3(3) expressly excludes written communications in respect of proceedings of a judicial authority.

misconceptions.trap: Any letter sent to a last known address is automatically deemed received.
misconceptions.correction: The alternative route requires reasonable inquiry establishing that the specified current places cannot be found and requires the statutory delivery method.

misconceptions.trap: Section 3 always overrides an agreed communication procedure.
misconceptions.correction: Section 3(1) expressly begins with “Unless otherwise agreed by the parties”.

misconceptions.trap: Section 3 applies equally to court communications.
misconceptions.correction: Section 3(3) expressly excludes communications concerning proceedings of a judicial authority.

questionsAndAnswers.question: What must be established to rely on section 3 for deemed receipt?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: Identify the arbitral communication, check whether the parties agreed to a different method, establish the applicable delivery route under section 3(1), prove the delivery record and, where section 3(1)(b) is invoked, establish the required reasonable inquiry. Section 3(2) then fixes the deemed date of receipt as the day of delivery.
questionsAndAnswers.explanation: The statutory sequence should be applied in order.

questionsAndAnswers.question: How should a party defend reliance on section 3(1)(b)?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: The submission should identify the addresses specified in section 3(1)(a), demonstrate the reasonable inquiry undertaken to locate them, identify the last known address, prove use of registered letter or another means providing a record of the delivery attempt, and explain why the communication is within the arbitral proceeding rather than a judicial-authority proceeding.
questionsAndAnswers.explanation: Each statutory precondition should be tied to documentary evidence.

bareActPointers: Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 — section 3(1)(a) and (b)
examTips: Start with the statutory phrase “Unless otherwise agreed by the parties”.
Distinguish the ordinary delivery route from the last-known-address route.
Prove reasonable inquiry before invoking section 3(1)(b).
Check section 3(3) before applying deemed receipt to a judicial communication.

Section 3(1)(a) covers personal delivery and delivery at specified addresses.
Section 3(1)(b) requires reasonable inquiry before the last-known-address route.
Section 3(2) fixes the deemed receipt date as the day of delivery.

essentialIngredients: Communication falls within the arbitral proceeding.
No contrary party agreement displaces the default rule, or the agreed method is identified.
For section 3(1)(a), delivery is to the person or specified place.
For section 3(1)(b), none of the specified places can be found after reasonable inquiry.
For section 3(1)(b), the communication is sent by the prescribed recorded-delivery method.
The communication is not excluded under section 3(3).
